title: Student Engagement with GenAI’s Tutoring Feedback: A Mixed Methods Study
venue: Koli Calling '25 / Proceedings of the 25th International Conference on Computing Education Research
extended_summary:
This paper investigates how students engage with immediate AI-generated tutoring feedback in programming education. The authors focus on a gap in prior work: while many studies examine the quality of GenAI feedback, less is known about whether students actually notice, understand, and use that feedback during problem solving.

To study this, the authors built a Python learning environment in which students could request four distinct GenAI tutoring feedback components: identifying problems, providing explanations/examples, giving a next-step hint, and offering a strategic approach. The feedback was generated with GPT-4.1 and integrated into Tutor Kai. Students used the system while working on Python exercises that matched an introductory programming course. The study combined think-aloud protocols, eye-tracking, screen recordings, and questionnaire data.

The study involved 20 undergraduate students in an introductory programming course at a German university. The tasks were part of a course environment used during the summer semester, and the participants were mostly first- or second-semester students. The results show that students often understood or agreed with the feedback, but a substantial portion of their thoughts indicated they needed more information, thought the feedback was irrelevant, or judged it as not helpful. When students expressed understanding, they were more likely to improve their code; when they expressed disagreement or needed more information, they often collected another feedback component instead of acting immediately.

Overall, the paper concludes that students are active, selective consumers of GenAI tutoring feedback rather than passive recipients. The authors argue that systems should better support follow-up clarification, because students frequently evaluate feedback against their own internal understanding before deciding whether to act on it.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative mixed-methods study with think-aloud, eye-tracking, and screen-recording analysis rather than a causal impact evaluation. It is methodologically careful and includes inter-coder reliability, but it does not meet higher-evidence experimental standards.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports descriptive, process-oriented findings about how students engage with GenAI feedback rather than a measured educational impact with effect sizes. Its implications are useful for design, but the demonstrated outcome impact on learning is unclear and modest at best.

interventions.use_case: GenAI-generated tutoring feedback for introductory Python programming tasks, delivered through four feedback components (find problems, explanations/examples, next-step hints, and strategic approach) in an online practice environment using GPT-4.1 with structured prompts and RAG-supported lecture links.

AI-generated immediate tutoring feedback on students' code submissions, with separate feedback components for error diagnosis, concept explanation, actionable next-step hints, and strategic problem-solving guidance.

finding.finding_summary: The study found that students' feedback engagement reflected self-regulation, internal evaluation, and metacognitive decision-making. Students often judged whether feedback was relevant, already known, or required more detail before acting; when they expressed understanding, 76.2% of related feedback components led to code improvements, but disagreement or missing-information thoughts often led to no immediate action and seeking more feedback instead.
finding.measure: Think-aloud coded themes, feedback-selection behavior, and immediate coding actions after reading AI feedback components

finding.finding_summary: Students' engagement showed signs of help-seeking, frustration, and perceived usefulness across feedback types. Of 380 collected and read feedback components, students explicitly judged feedback as helpful 26 times and not helpful 32 times; when feedback seemed irrelevant or insufficient, they commonly collected another component rather than acting immediately.
finding.measure: Think-aloud judgments of helpfulness/not helpfulness, feedback collection rates, and no-action rates
